opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and one I think about a lot, because it would be a bit hypocritical to point out the problems with sparse autoencoders and then pretend our own approach is immune to the same kinds of critique.

The core worry I have about SAEs is that they decompose *activations* rather than the *mechanisms* themselves. You get a dictionary of directions that reconstruct the activations reasonably well, but there's no guarantee those directions correspond to the things the network actually computes with. You see feature splitting, absorption, dead latents, and a reconstruction error that's doing a lot of unexplained work. You end up with a description of the representation, but not obviously of the computation.

Parameter decomposition tries to address that by decomposing the weights into components, asking which small subset of mechanisms is needed on any given input, while summing back to the original parameters. That gives us a more principled tie to what the network is doing.

But it has its own limits, and I'd name a few honestly.

First, scalability. These methods are more expensive and harder to train than SAEs. We've made real progress, but we're not yet at the frontier models people most care about, and until we are, a lot of what I'm saying is a bet rather than a demonstrated result.

Second, hyperparameter sensitivity and the choice of objective. Any decomposition method smuggles in assumptions, about what counts as "simple," how you measure whether a component is causally important, how you trade off faithfulness against minimality. If those assumptions are wrong, you can get clean-looking components that are artifacts of the objective. That's exactly the critique I make of SAEs, and it applies to us too.

Third, there's a deeper conceptual question about whether networks really decompose into a modest number of crisp mechanisms at all. Maybe a lot of what models do is genuinely distributed and messy, and any method that assumes a sparse, modular structure will be forcing that structure onto the model. I don't think we know yet, and I'd like to be in a position where our methods could tell us we're wrong.

And finally, interpretability of the components themselves. Even if you get a faithful decomposition, you still need humans, or automated tools, to understand what each component means, and that labeling step has its own failure modes.

So my honest assessment is: I think moving from activations toward parameters is the right direction, and I'd defend it. But I hold it as a research bet, with open problems I'm trying to make visible rather than paper over. The field went through a phase of being quite excited about SAEs before the limitations were properly appreciated, and I'd rather we not repeat that pattern with whatever comes next, including our own work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limitations of SAEs and the proposed parameter decomposition, but does not say that criticisms of SAEs may not apply to other variants of sparse dictionary learning.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether its decomposition assumptions and objectives yield genuine mechanisms, noting that they could produce components that are artifacts rather than what the method intends to identify.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and I think the honest answer is that a lot of the criticisms I've leveled at SAEs apply, in some form, to what we're doing too. Let me try to lay that out.

The core critique of sparse autoencoders, from my side, was never really "this is a bad method." It was that SAEs are optimizing a proxy. You're training a dictionary to reconstruct activations sparsely, and you're hoping that the sparse directions you get correspond to the computational units the network actually uses. But reconstruction plus sparsity is a statement about the activation distribution, not about the mechanism. You can carve up a representation in lots of ways that reconstruct well and look interpretable, and nothing in the objective guarantees that the pieces you get are the pieces the model is actually computing with. Feature splitting, feature absorption, the fact that you get different dictionaries at different widths, all of that is a symptom of the same underlying issue.

So with parameter decomposition, what we've tried to do is move the question from "what structure is in the activations" to "what structure is in the computation." Decompose the weights into components, and ask that the model's behaviour on any given input be explained by as few of those components as possible, while still being faithful to the original network. That's a different objective and I think it's a more principled one, because it's at least pointing at mechanism rather than at representation.

But here's where I have to be honest about the limits. First, we've also got a proxy. "Minimal description length of the mechanism used on this input" is a nice idea, but what we actually optimize is a tractable approximation involving attributions and sparsity penalties, and those approximations can be gamed by the optimizer just like SAE objectives can. We've seen components that look clean on toy models and we don't yet have strong evidence that this scales to frontier-sized networks without the decomposition becoming ugly in ways we don't anticipate.

Second, the toy-model problem. Most of the clean results in this space, ours included, come from settings where we built the ground truth and then checked whether the method recovers it. That's the right place to start, but it's a very weak form of validation. Real models don't come with a ground truth, and when you don't have one, you're back to using the same kind of qualitative, "does this look interpretable" evaluation that I've criticized SAE work for leaning on too heavily.

Third, there are things the framework just doesn't handle well yet. Attention is awkward. Anything where the relevant mechanism is distributed across many parameters in a way that doesn't respect the component boundaries we're imposing is going to be hard. And there's a deeper worry about whether networks are actually decomposable in the way the approach presumes. Maybe the right description of some computations is genuinely holistic, and any method that insists on splitting into discrete parts is going to produce artifacts.

So the way I try to assess it is: the test is not whether components look nice. The test is whether the decomposition lets you do something you couldn't do before. Predict a behaviour you hadn't observed, remove a capability surgically, find a mechanism you weren't looking for. We've got early signs on some of that, and I'd say we're clearly short of being able to claim it robustly.

I think the meta-point is that the field, me included, needs to stop grading methods on how interpretable the outputs seem and start grading them on downstream tasks with real stakes. If I'm not willing to apply that standard to my own work, I don't get to apply it to anyone else's.

r001.rationale: The response discusses criticisms of sparse autoencoders and a distinct parameter-decomposition approach, but does not say those criticisms may not apply to other variants of sparse dictionary learning.

r002.rationale: It says the method optimizes a proxy that can be gamed and that there is not yet strong evidence it scales or reliably recovers mechanisms in real models.

astra-6.text:
I think the criticisms have to apply to my own approach as well. If I’m skeptical that sparse autoencoders recover the right units for understanding a model, I can’t just propose a different decomposition and assume that its components are the real ones. That’s something you have to establish empirically.

There are a few distinct questions here. Can you reconstruct the model’s activations? Can you give the components plausible interpretations? And can you use those interpretations to predict what the model will do, particularly when you intervene on it or change the input distribution? Success on the first two doesn’t necessarily imply success on the third.

So I’d treat my approach as a hypothesis about what might make model computation easier to understand. It will have its own assumptions, and those assumptions will make some kinds of structure easier to find and others harder to find. The danger is that you end up seeing what your method is designed to reveal, and mistake that for a complete account.

What would give me confidence is being able to make specific, falsifiable predictions about the model and then test them. Even then, I’d distinguish understanding a particular mechanism from having enough understanding to make a safety claim about the whole system. That’s a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: The response says the criticisms should apply to the speaker’s own approach too, but does not state that they may not apply to other variants of sparse dictionary learning.

r002.rationale: The response treats the approach as a hypothesis, says its components cannot be assumed to be the real ones, and says this must be established empirically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the same skepticism has to apply to our own work. It’s quite easy to find something that looks interpretable and then mistake that for having understood what the model is doing. My criticism of sparse autoencoders isn’t that they’re useless; it’s that the evidence you get from them can be weaker than the conclusions you’re tempted to draw.

For our approach, too, there are assumptions about what the right units of explanation are and what kinds of structure we should look for. Those assumptions could be wrong, or they could work in some settings and fail in others. And an explanation that captures one part of a computation may leave out something essential.

So I’d want to distinguish finding useful structure from having a faithful account of the computation. The stronger test is whether that account makes predictions: can we anticipate what happens under interventions, explain failures, and identify where the explanation stops working? Until we can do that reliably, I’d treat our results as partial evidence rather than a complete understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says skepticism should apply to the guest’s own work too, but does not distinguish other variants of sparse dictionary learning from sparse autoencoders.

r002.rationale: The response says the approach’s assumptions about the right explanatory units and structures could be wrong, and treats its results as partial evidence. This acknowledges uncertainty about whether the approach finds what it is intended to find.
